new_statements.quote: The present writer has information from his own fieldnotes, on the structures of Nambu and Iauga (Parb) which are virtually identical. The following notes reflect only their features. The phonology is quite complex, and the following statements are also tentative. [...] Vowel length is phonemic. Several diphthongs are found. The suprasegmental system appears to consist of a relatively complex stress system with rhythm principles, but no tonal system seems to be present. The syllable structure is of some complexity.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nambu and Iauga (Parb) have a stress system described only as 'relatively complex' and governed by 'rhythm principles' (i.e. rhythmic/alternating stress), with no tone; the position of primary stress is not stated and the author flags the phonological statements as tentative.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Implied only by 'rhythm principles' (alternating rhythm); nothing explicit.
new_statements.identity_note: The notes are stated to cover 'Nambu and Iauga (Parb)', whose structures Wurm found 'virtually identical', from his own 1970 fieldnotes. Iauga = the village Iauga on Strachan Island (25 speakers, sec. 3.35.11.12, p. 152), which Wurm identifies with Riley & Ray's Parb; Usher (New Guinea World) files Parb (Ray 1923; Riley 1930-31) under Län = lenn1234, and Evans et al. give Tais (the present Len village) as 'originally Yaoga' (= Iauga). So Iauga (Parb) is very probably Len; but the statement is a joint Nambu-subfamily note (Wurm's 'Nambu' = the Nambo/Namat/Nama/Namo chain, other glottocodes), lexicostatistically he treats Iauga as a near-dialect of Nambu (83%), and Rueck 2011 doubts any linguist visited Iauga after 1930. Not the Tais 'Nambu-Dorro transition dialect' (that is Namo/Nä). | Stock-level generalisation over all Trans-Fly Stock languages; the stock's Nambu Sub-Family is listed as 'Nambu, Iauga (Parb), Dorro' (p. 329 list; p. 330 'Iauga (or Parb) is apparently a dialect of Nambu'). Iauga/Parb = Län per Usher and Ray 1923's Parb Group (Glottolog's hh note instead codes it Nambo [ncm]). Glottolog attaches the chapter to namo1246 and the other Trans-Fly languages, not to lenn1234. Even if the identity holds, the statement is a template shared by c. 25 languages and gives no stress position.

new_statements.quote: In general, the languages of the Trans-Fly Stock display a good measure of typological and structural similarity, and share a considerable number of features. On the phonological level, they all share a suprasegmental system which manifests itself in a complex stress system with rhythm principles, and in addition, the languages of the Kiwaian and Eastern Trans-Fly Families seem to possess a two-tone system with usually low to very low functional load.
